My research focuses on the ecological processes that drive the distribution and abundance of animal populations. I combine fieldwork, large-scale data synthesis (bird ringing, citizen science), and quantitative modelling to tackle questions across spatial and temporal scales.

## Understanding and forecasting where species live, and how that is changing
:::

::: {.lines}

### [Movement and the geography of species](dispersal.qmd)

Animals move at every scale, from a morning's foraging to a lifetime's dispersal, and those movements set where populations persist, how connected they are and how fast ranges can shift. I study how individual movement scales up to population and range dynamics, and why individuals of the same species differ so much in how far they go.

Dispersal drives almost everything in ecology, yet for most species we simply do not know how far individuals disperse. With collaborators I developed Bayesian methods that account for the biases in bird ringing data and produced standardised dispersal kernels for over 200 European bird species. I am now exploring why dispersal varies so much *within* species.

### [Biodiversity modelling and forecasting](forecasting.qmd)

Most models of species distributions describe where a species is found, not the processes that put it there. I develop models that carry ecological process explicitly — dispersal, population dynamics, species interactions, imperfect detection — and that integrate heterogeneous data, so that forecasts of biodiversity change rest on mechanism rather than correlation.

Each data type has biases, but combining them thoughtfully can give a more complete picture of both spatial coverage and temporal dynamics.

### [Conservation under global change](conservation.qmd)

Habitat loss and climate change are redrawing species distributions. I work on anticipating which species are most exposed and why, and on turning that understanding into spatial priorities: where and when problems will emerge, and where intervention is most likely to matter.

This includes large carnivore range expansion in Iberia, occupancy models that correct for preferential sampling in threatened species assessments, and applied work on Mediterranean river ecosystems and bat habitat modelling.

### [Monitoring biodiversity at scale](../outreach.qmd#field-technology)

Good inference needs good observation. I work on how autonomous sensors, citizen science and long-term surveys can be designed and combined to monitor wildlife at the scales that conservation decisions require, and on the analytical pipelines that turn raw observations into evidence.

Camera trapping, bioacoustic monitoring (using AudioMoth devices), and other sensor-based approaches for wildlife monitoring. I am developing field technology pipelines for biodiversity assessment in collaboration with [Raúl Bonal](https://scholar.google.es/citations?user=xKxS6YIAAAAJ) on bioacoustics.

## Big datasets and quantitative methods
:::

::: {.line .no-fig}
::: {.rail}
[Data and methods]{.kicker}
:::
::: {.text}
- **Ring-recovery data** from EURING and national schemes, one of the largest individual-level animal movement datasets in the world
- **Citizen science observations** (especially eBird)
- **Bayesian hierarchical models** implemented in R
- **Camera trapping and bioacoustic monitoring** in the field

I am committed to open science. Code and data for my papers are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/guifandos) and archived on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/search?q=fandos).
:::
